hook: In eighteen fifty-nine, the night sky turned red over Cuba.

blocks.narration: In eighteen fifty-nine, the night sky turned red over Cuba, and telegraph wires started sparking across two continents at the same time.
blocks.visual: A night sky glowing deep red above palm trees and a small colonial town, people in 1850s clothing pointing up

blocks.narration: On September first, astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots when two blinding white flashes erupted from the Sun's surface.
blocks.visual: A 19th century astronomer at a brass telescope projecting the Sun onto paper, two brilliant white flashes on the projected disc

blocks.narration: It was the first solar flare anyone had ever recorded. About seventeen hours later, a giant magnetic storm slammed into Earth.
blocks.visual: A huge glowing cloud of plasma leaving the Sun and racing toward a tiny blue Earth across dark space

blocks.narration: Auroras glowed so brightly that people in the northeastern United States could read newspapers by their light at midnight.
blocks.visual: People in 1850s clothing standing in a town square at midnight holding folded papers, lit by bright green and red auroras

blocks.narration: Telegraph operators got electric shocks, and some lines kept sending messages for two hours with their batteries completely disconnected.
blocks.visual: A 19th century telegraph office with sparks jumping from the wires and an operator pulling his hand back in surprise

blocks.narration: Scientists call it the Carrington Event, the strongest geomagnetic storm on record. A storm like that today could damage satellites and power grids.
blocks.visual: Modern satellites and a glowing city power grid under a huge shimmering aurora, lights flickering

blocks.narration: That is why scientists still study one strange night when the Sun reached out and touched Earth. It all began
blocks.visual: The calm Sun rising over a quiet 19th century observatory at dawn, soft golden light

captions.hook_line: 1859: the sky turned red and telegraph wires caught fire. The Carrington Event 🌌
captions.body: On September 1, 1859, Richard Carrington recorded the first solar flare. Hours later the strongest geomagnetic storm on record lit up skies as far south as Cuba and shocked telegraph operators.
